Below is a concise, evidence‑backed explanation of how “digital skills” differ between the general workforce and technology jobs, plus how they overlap and how to build them in practice.

Summary: what differs
- Scope of work dictates scope of skills. Digital skills in tech roles focus on creating/maintaining digital systems (coding, DevOps, data/ML, security architecture), while general‑workforce roles emphasize using digital tools to perform business tasks (communication, collaboration, customer workflows, office automation) and applying digital literacy to job processes. <cite id="fef97483-0">OECD distinguishes ICT specialists who develop, operate, and maintain ICT systems; advanced users who master sector‑specific software; and basic users of generic tools for work and society</cite> <cite id="fef97483-1">A widely used framework (DigComp 2.1) organizes digital competences into information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving</cite> <cite id="fef97483-4">The European Commission groups digital skills into basic literacy, ICT‑for‑employment (on‑the‑job ICT competences), and ICT‑professional skills (innovative/creative competences to design new digital solutions)</cite>.
- Depth and complexity rise in tech roles. Tech jobs often require specialist activities like software development and ICT architecture design, while general roles typically operate at advanced usage levels (e.g., design, simulation, workflow automation) rather than writing low‑level code or system architecture. <cite id="fef97483-4">OECD activity tiers range from basic mouse/Internet use and email to advanced software design/simulation and specialist software development/architecture</cite> <cite id="fef97483-0">Advanced users are competent with sector‑specific tools; basic users with generic tools; ICT specialists develop and maintain systems</cite>.
- Soft skills are universal complements. Across both groups, critical thinking, problem solving, communication, teamwork, and project management are emphasized; in tech, these are paired with technical depth; in general roles, they are paired with tool fluency and process integration. <cite id="fef97483-0">Soft skills like critical thinking, problem solving, project management, and teamwork are repeatedly identified as key for ICT professionals</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-1">Cybersecurity job analyses show both technical skills (network traffic, OS hardening) and non‑technical skills (communication, teamwork, problem solving) are in demand</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-2">Data science/software postings highlight communication, collaboration, and presentation alongside technical tasks</cite>.

How digital skills are defined and categorized
- Policy frameworks converge on a layered view. <cite id="fef97483-1">DigComp 2.1’s five areas—information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving—provide cross‑sector competences with proficiency levels recognized by OECD, UNESDOC, ITU, and the European Commission</cite>. <cite id="fef97483-4">The European Commission’s broad definition frames digital skills as the ability to locate, organize, understand, develop, create, and disseminate information using digital technologies, with levels from basic literacy to ICT‑professional competences</cite>. <cite id="fef97483-0">OECD’s three ICT skill categories (specialists, advanced users, basic users) map to creators/maintainers vs. users across society and work</cite>. <cite id="fef97483-3">OECD’s “Skills for a Digital World” calls out technical/professional, ICT generic skills, and soft skills (leadership, communication, teamwork), and urges early acquisition of basic ICT and continuous upskilling</cite>.
- Crosswalk to occupations: policy tools connect skills to jobs. <cite id="fef97483-2">ESCO integrates DigComp into occupation profiles, while job analytics show that 44% of Europeans lack basic digital skills and that 9 out of 10 jobs will require digital competences; there remains a shortage of 500,000 ICT experts in the EU</cite>.

Core differences in competencies and tasks
- Tooling and tasks
  - General workforce: daily fluency with collaboration suites, customer‑facing platforms, ERP/CRM, spreadsheets/BI, and workflow automation; translating business needs into digital processes. <cite id="302ce59f-1">Hospitality postings emphasize communication across email, instant messaging, and customer management platforms, plus operational use of hotel management software and office packages</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-3">Retail “connected service encounters” introduce new shopfloor tasks and roles that require workplace learning in digital tools; low literacy, numeracy, computer, and digital skills put entry‑level workers at risk of marginalization</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-4">Retail banking digitization reduces branches and reshapes job profiles; frontline workers must combine traditional relational skills with digital competences aligned to new strategic objectives</cite>.
  - Tech jobs: design, build, and maintain systems; programming, data engineering/ML, DevOps, security hardening and monitoring; integrating APIs and architecture. <cite id="fef97483-0">ICT specialists develop, operate, and maintain ICT systems and advanced sector‑specific software tools</cite> <cite id="fef97483-4">Advanced activities include writing code, design/simulation, and specialist software development and architecture</cite>.
- Depth and autonomy
  - General workforce: advanced and specialist‑adjacent tasks are common (automation, dashboards, integration), but decisions sit at the business problem level rather than system‑level design. <cite id="fef97483-4">Advanced activities (design, simulation, programming) contrast with specialist activities (software development, architecture) and basic activities (email, copying files, simple browsing)</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-0">Digitization shifts demand from basic ICT toward when/why to use tools for complex cognitive and metacognitive work, requiring balanced soft and technical proficiency</cite>.
  - Tech jobs: hands‑on coding and infrastructure tasks are routine, often with ownership of reliability, security, and performance; higher cognitive load in debugging, algorithm design, and system architecture. <cite id="fef97483-0">ICT specialists develop/operate/maintain systems and advanced sector tools</cite> <cite id="fef97483-4">Specialist activities include software development and ICT architecture design for the workplace</cite>.
- Data, AI, and security emphasis
  - General workforce: data literacy to interpret dashboards, validate inputs/outputs, and communicate insights; privacy/sharing controls in customer and HR systems; process hygiene (backup, versioning, SLA adherence). <cite id="fef97483-1">Information/data literacy and safety/problem solving are core DigComp areas</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-1">Operational digital skills (hotel systems) plus communication across digital channels are central in hospitality</cite>.
  - Tech jobs: statistical modeling, ML engineering, pipelines, and security hardening/operations dominate; compliance and risk analysis are integral to design and maintenance. <cite id="a6947c3e-2">Data science job postings highlight soft skills alongside technical tasks</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-1">Cybersecurity roles demand both technical skills (networking, OS hardening) and communication/presentation/collaboration</cite>.
- Soft skills as glue
  - Both need critical thinking, problem solving, teamwork, and continuous learning; tech roles lean on these to decompose system problems, while general roles use them to optimize workflows and customer experiences. <cite id="fef97483-0">Critical thinking, project management, teamwork are repeatedly identified as key soft skills for ICT professionals</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-1">Cybersecurity postings emphasize communication, teamwork, and problem solving alongside technical requirements</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-2">Data/AI postings foreground collaboration and presentation within technical work</cite>.

Sectoral snapshots: how general roles use digital skills
- Customer service and retail
  - Core digital tasks: routing tickets, managing live chat, CRM updates, inventory/point‑of‑sale, and omnichannel comms; these require cross‑platform fluency and emotional labor plus responsiveness. <cite id="302ce59f-1">Receptionist roles in hospitality demand communication via email/WhatsApp/customer platforms and operational use of hotel management software; internet/email/online telephony/social media are more common than metasearch</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-3">In retail, connected service encounters bring new shopfloor tasks and roles; workers act as enablers/translation/coordinators at checkout, yet traditional “organic dialogue” practices persist alongside new technology</cite>.
- Healthcare and education services
  - Core digital tasks: scheduling, electronic records, telehealth, learning management systems, and data entry/reporting; competences include digital health literacy and safe, ethical use of AI. <cite id="302ce59f-2">Nursing students reported robust understanding and positive attitudes toward digital transformation and AI, with strong digital skills applicable in daily life and labor markets, and positive correlations between knowledge of digital services and digital variables</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-0">Across services, digitalization changes job design by demanding alignment of machine learning with human reasoning; efficiency and effectiveness in data/information processing require knowing when/why/how to use digital tools for complex cognitive work</cite>.
- Professional services and finance
  - Core digital tasks: document automation, knowledge management, analytics, compliance dashboards; traditional relational/analytical skills are “re‑skilled” with digital methods. <cite id="302ce59f-4">Retail banking digitization reduces branches and redefines customer‑facing and central office roles; traditional skills must combine with digital ones to align with new strategic objectives, amid managerialization, globalization, and intensification that raise stress and identity issues</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-1">In hospitality, digital communication (email/WhatsApp) and operational systems (hotel management software) are central, with employers prioritizing communication and operational digital skills over purely informational ones during hiring</cite>.

Overlap and progression pathways
- Overlap is substantial. <cite id="fef97483-0">Advanced users and ICT professionals both need communication, collaboration, and problem solving; the boundary blurs as non‑tech roles adopt advanced tools (e.g., spreadsheets, CRM, ERP) and data visualization</cite> <cite id="fef97483-1">DigComp competences (information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, problem solving) apply across roles</cite>.
- Bridge skills and credentials. <cite id="fef97483-2">ESCO’s alignment with DigComp supports mapping general competences to occupation profiles, while upskilling demand is high: by 2022, 54% of the existing workforce was projected to need upskilling or reskilling</cite> <cite id="fef97483-4">OECD policy emphasizes ensuring basic ICT in initial education and continuous reskilling/upskilling as demands evolve</cite>. In practice, micro‑credentials and bootcamps target the “adjacent specialist” gap: <cite id="fef97483-0">advanced sector‑specific software use for general roles, and programming/networking for ICT roles</cite>.
- Security and privacy basics are now baseline for all. <cite id="fef97483-1">Safety/problem solving and data literacy are core competences</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-1">Security postings consistently foreground both technical hardening and non‑technical communication/collaboration</cite>.

What “how it is” looks like in practice
- General workforce
  - Who does it: non‑IT employees in admin, customer care, HR, retail, hospitality, education, healthcare, finance, and professional services. <cite id="fef97483-0">Basic and advanced users comprise the majority of digital tool adopters in society and work</cite> <cite id="fef97483-2">ESCO profiles integrate DigComp into occupational competence requirements</cite>.
  - What they need: 
    - Core: file management, search, email with attachments, collaboration suites, customer platforms, ERP/CRM, spreadsheets/BI, and safety/problem solving. <cite id="fef97483-4">Low/basic activities include mouse use, downloading browsers, copying files, sending email with attachments</cite> <cite id="fef97483-1">Communication/collaboration, information literacy, and safety/problem solving are foundational</cite>.
    - Adjacent: dashboards, workflow automation, API integrations, and basic scripting to augment roles; soft skills to analyze processes, empathize with users, and train peers. <cite id="302ce59f-0">Balancing soft and technical skills is imperative as tools mediate complex cognitive work</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-1">Operational digital skills plus cross‑channel communication are highly valued; employers report these as key for performance and satisfaction</cite>.
  - What’s missing vs tech: less system design/coding and more business translation, governance, and customer outcomes; however, exposure to data/ML concepts improves impact. <cite id="fef97483-4">Specialist activities (software development and architecture) sit at the ICT‑professional level rather than general roles</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-2">Data/AI jobs reward communication and collaboration alongside technical tasks</cite>.
- Tech jobs
  - Who does it: software engineers, data/ML engineers, DevOps/SRE, network/security engineers, architects, data scientists. <cite id="fef97483-0">ICT specialists develop/operate/maintain systems and advanced sector tools</cite>.
  - What they need: 
    - Core: programming, algorithms/data structures, software design patterns, testing/debugging; data engineering, ML/DS pipelines; cloud/DevOps toolchains; networking/security hardening. <cite id="fef97483-4">Advanced activities include writing code, design/simulation; specialist activities include software development and ICT architecture design</cite>.
    - Adjacent: communication, teamwork, project management, and documentation to translate requirements into systems. <cite id="fef97483-0">Soft skills like critical thinking, problem solving, project management, and teamwork are crucial for ICT professionals</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-1">Cybersecurity roles repeatedly require communication, presentation, and collaboration alongside technical skills</cite>.
  - What’s missing vs general: more system‑level thinking, performance/security trade‑offs, compliance, CI/CD automation, and continuous learning to keep pace with frameworks and languages; still, strong general‑purpose problem solving and cross‑functional communication are prerequisites. <cite id="fef97483-3">OECD stresses continuous reskilling/upskilling as job demands change</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-1">Hands‑on skills are highly valued across technical roles</cite>.

How to build the right skills in your context
- Diagnose job tasks first. <cite id="fef97483-2">Use occupation frameworks (e.g., ESCO with DigComp alignment) to map required competences to tasks and proficiency levels, then identify gaps</cite> <cite id="fef97483-1">Prioritize information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving aligned to your workflows</cite>.
- Layer competences:
  - General workforce: start with core digital fluency (files, search, email, collaboration suites), then add domain tools (CRM/ERP), data literacy (dashboards, KPI validation), and customer‑workflow automation; invest in communication/empathy and change management. <cite id="302ce59f-1">Email/online telephony/IM, customer platforms, and hotel management software are concrete entry points in hospitality; communication skills are most sought after</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-3">Frontline service digitalization increases the need for workplace learning in digital tools; weak digital skills jeopardize entry‑level roles</cite>.
  - Tech jobs: build from problem decomposition and design to programming/DS/DevOps; pair code sprints with security reviews and documentation; emphasize teamwork and communication to bridge technical and business stakeholders. <cite id="fef97483-0">Advanced users progress toward specialist competences in sector‑specific software; ICT specialists develop/operate/maintain systems</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-1">Technical skills must be paired with communication, collaboration, and problem solving</cite>.
- Close the widening gap. <cite id="fef97483-2">Given projections that 54% of the existing workforce will need upskilling by 2022 and persistent shortages of hundreds of thousands of ICT experts, targeted upskilling is strategic for both workers and employers</cite> <cite id="fef97483-3">OECD’s policy guidance emphasizes ensuring basic ICT in initial education, aligning curricula to skill needs, and motivating continuous upskilling across employers and employees</cite>.
- Measure outcomes with simple proxies. <cite id="302ce59f-1">In hospitality, digital communication and operational system skills were strongly linked to customer satisfaction and efficiency, making them top requirements in postings</cite> <cite id="302ce59f-2">In education/healthcare, positive attitudes toward digital transformation and AI correlated with stronger digital variables among students, suggesting training that builds both knowledge and comfort yields measurable gains</cite>.

Remaining uncertainties
- Market dynamics shift quickly. Platform analytics show tech roles concentrate hiring, but demand varies by economy and sector; job‑posting snapshots can skew toward higher‑skilled roles. <cite id="a6947c3e-3">Technology & IT accounted for 33.7% of 1,000 LinkedIn job postings analyzed across 14 professional domains, reflecting concentration of tech roles in the current digital economy</cite> <cite id="a6947c3e-0">A one‑day LinkedIn crawl provides a valuable snapshot but does not represent all jobs; role selection (e.g., prompt engineer, data roles) shapes observed skill requirements</cite>.
- Return on investment depends on alignment. <cite id="fef97483-2">While 44% of Europeans lack basic digital skills and 9 out of 10 jobs require digital competences,ESCO does not indicate proficiency levels, making gap analysis job‑specific</cite>. Evidence suggests balancing soft and technical skills is critical for sustainable impact. <cite id="302ce59f-0">Balancing soft and technical skills is imperative in the era of technological transformation, as digitalization changes job designs across services</cite>.

Bottom line
- Think of digital skills as a pyramid: general workforce roles need a wide base of practical, job‑embedded competences to operate, analyze, and improve processes with digital tools, while tech jobs require climbing higher on the pyramid to design, build, and operate systems; both share the same apex of soft skills and responsibility. <cite id="fef97483-4">Basic activities (email, file ops) support advanced (design/simulation, programming) and specialist activities (software development, architecture)</cite> <cite id="fef97483-1">Information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving are transferable across roles</cite> <cite id="fef97483-0">Advanced users and ICT specialists differ in what they build and maintain versus use, but both rely on communication, collaboration, and problem solving</cite>.

Other frameworks prioritize 21st century digital skills that allow citizens to leverage ICTs through skills like critical thinking, problem-solving, communication, collaboration, and safety (Economou, 2016;Ferrari, 2012;Iordache, et al., 2017;Law, et al., 2018;Wedlake et al., 2019).

• Digital skills for the ICT professions. They cover both of the above-mentioned categories and skills required in the ICT field and bringing in innovative and creative components for the development of new digital solutions, products or services.

Title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
Snippet: For this study, we use a dataset of job postings scraped from LinkedIn on April 7, 2025. The one-day crawl provides us a snapshot view into the online job market on this given date. While job postings on LinkedIn do not reflect all jobs advertised online, LinkedIn represents one of the largest global platforms for professional networking and job advertisements, making it a valuable source for analyzing current labor market trends. The data was crawled across the 60 countries with the most technological expertise, based on the U.S. News & World Report rankings (U.S. News, 2025). The countries are listed in the supplemental material. The distribution of jobs reflects the concentration of tech jobs world-wide. For our comparative analysis, we selected four job roles for being highly relevant and potentially overlapping with the role of prompt engineer. Title: Employees’ Competitiveness in Digital Transformation
Snippet: We first clarify the concept of "digital skills" and "digital competencies", because there is no single definition of digital skills and competencies. There are many different interpretations related to the ability to use information and communication technologies (ICT) such as digital literacy, digital competence, computer literacy, e-skills (electronic skills), information literacy and others. 

There are different classifications of digital skills supposed by van Laar, E. et al [2], European Commission [3], OECD [4], European Schoolnet and DIGITALEUROPE [5], Development Economics [6] and Carretero, S. et al [7]. We have chosen the most actual for our study. 

According to experts of the European Commission, in a broad sense, digital skills mean the ability to localize, organize, understand, develop, create and disseminate information using digital technologies at different levels of competence [8]. The European Commission defines three levels of digital skills: 

• Basic digital literacy skills. They allow individuals acquire digital literacy. These skills can be used both in the workplace and in the personal life of an individual to increase the level of knowledge and involvement in the digital community. 

• Digital skills which relate to employment. They include basic digital skills, as well as on-the-job and related to information and communication technologies (ICT), developed by information technology professionals. 

• Digital skills for the ICT professions. They cover both of the above-mentioned categories and skills required in the ICT field and bringing in innovative and creative components for the development of new digital solutions, products or services. 

OECD [9] allocates: 

• Low and basic activities. Using a computer mouse to download an Internet browser, copying or moving files, using copying tools, cutting and pasting information on the screen, using search engines to request information, sending an email with file attachments and others. 

•Advanced activities. Writing code in a programming language, using software for design, counting or simulation, programming and using robots. 

• Specialist activities. Software development, ICT architecture design for the workplace. UKforCE [10] offers the following levels: 

• Digital Muggle. There are no requirements for using digital technologies -they are perceived as magic. 

• Digital Citizen.

Title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
Snippet: For this study, we use a dataset of job postings scraped from LinkedIn on April 7, 2025. The one-day crawl provides us a snapshot view into the online job market on this given date. While job postings on LinkedIn do not reflect all jobs advertised online, LinkedIn represents one of the largest global platforms for professional networking and job advertisements, making it a valuable source for analyzing current labor market trends. The data was crawled across the 60 countries with the most technological expertise, based on the U.S. News & World Report rankings (U.S. News, 2025). The countries are listed in the supplemental material. The distribution of jobs reflects the concentration of tech jobs world-wide. For our comparative analysis, we selected four job roles for being highly relevant and potentially overlapping with the role of prompt engineer. These job roles are data engineer, data analyst, machine learning engineer, and data scientist. 

The data collection was conducted in a two-step process: First we gathered all links to job postings that match the search criteria, then we extracted detailed information for each job posting. 

For identifying job roles, we searched for exact matches in job titles, using quoted keywords to ensure precise matching jobs (e.g., "prompt engineer"). This approach allowed us to create a precise snapshot of job market for these five roles at a specific point in time.

Title: Cybersecurity Study Programs: What's in a Name?
Snippet: Graham and Lu [17] analyzed 17,929 online job advertisements for cybersecurity positions. Apart from the requirements on technical skills, which were often focused on data (data protection, loss prevention, and privacy), the job postings strongly emphasized nontechnical skills, including communication, teamwork, and problemsolving. This is consistent with earlier work by Jones et al. [19] who interviewed 44 cyber professionals on the most important skills that cybersecurity students should learn in school. The technical skills included, for example, understanding how network traffic flows and how to harden operating systems. The non-technical skills included mainly communication, presentation skills, and collaboration. 

In a related work, Özyurt and Ayaz [43] analyzed 9,407 cybersecurity job postings. The advertised job roles were divided into ten categories (e.g., engineer, analyst, or manager), with each category further subdivided into specific job titles. In addition, automated topic modeling identified 23 topic categories (e.g., security operations, risk management, and business/customer services) within the job postings. The mapping between the job roles and the topics revealed which types of skills are more relevant for which types of positions, highlighting the spectrum between more technicallyoriented and more human/organization-oriented roles. 

Generally, the analysis of the current job market proves the importance of both technical and non-technical competencies, as well as the value of hands-on skills. This is strongly aligned with the cybersecurity curricular guidelines that we use as a baseline.

Title: Curious, Critical Thinker, Empathetic, and Ethically Responsible: Essential Soft Skills for Data Scientists in Software Engineering
Snippet: We conducted a systematic collection of data from job postings on the LinkedIn platform to pinpoint the most required soft skills from a market perspective. By utilizing one of the most prominent platforms for job postings, we were able to gather relevant, meaningful, and precise information about the soft skills that employers expect from professionals in the job market. 

In this process, we accessed LinkedIn and searched for job postings using the keywords Data Scientist, Soft Skills, and Software. Title: Digitalisation and valuations: an empirical analysis of valuers’ supplemental skills requirements
Snippet: As such, studies empirically exploring the impacts of digital innovations on skills requirements in the valuation profession are limited. Hence, this study explored literature in the services industry from healthcare to business administration (e.g. accounting, finance, auditing, management, and marketing) to understand the nature of general changes in the services industry to facilitate the primary research process. An overview of extant property literature on digitalisation and skills development is presented in Table 2. Overall, new technologies are changing job designs across the services industry, and these developments present challenges and potential for the workforce (see Figure 1). 

So, digitalisation will continue to challenge the mere acquisition of soft and technical skills as sustainable use of new technologies requires human interventions, and such circumstances require aligning machine learning with human reasoning. Therefore, the importance of soft skills lies in their irreplaceability, even in robotic environments. Consequently, a balance of proficiency in soft and technical skills is imperative in the era of technological transformation (Poláková et al., 2023). For now, there will continue to be an increasing demand for efficiency and effectiveness in extensive data and information processing capabilities, which means that the workforce needs to know why, when, and how to use digital tools and systems to perform jobs that involve complex cognitive and metacognitive skills instead of basic ICT skills (Chinien & Boutin, 2011).

Title: Analysis of The Interrelationship Between Employee's Digital Skills, Digitalization in Human Resource Management and Organizational Performance
Snippet: The study reveals that digital transformation has brought about significant changes in the hospitality industry, with digital skills becoming a key component of the sector's competencies. Job advertisements emphasize the importance of building good relationships with guests and meeting their needs through communication skills, which include direct interaction with customers via email, instant messaging applications, and customer management platforms. Operational skills, which involve using hotel management software and other digital systems, are the second most sought-after requirement, yet they significantly contribute to operational efficiency and customer satisfaction. On the other hand, employers view informational skills as supplementary rather than essential during the employee selection process. The most sought-after positions are receptionists, requiring strong communication skills and efficient operational abilities, while maintenance positions, with their more specific duties not directly related to the day-to-day guest experience, are in lower demand. Required technologies include hotel management systems and office equipment packages. The use of the internet and digital tools, such as email, online telephony, and social media, is more common than metasearch engines, with email and online telephony playing a significant role in internal and external communications and social media in promotions and customer interactions. The digital skills developed involve communication through various digital channels, with a focus on telephone, WhatsApp, and email, which are crucial for effective communication and responsiveness to guest needs. In conclusion, digital transformation highlights the importance of digital communication and operational skills in the hospitality sector, with hotel companies needing to adapt training programs and update job specifications to meet the evolving demands of the industry and reduce the skills gap.

Title: A Postdigital Perspective on Service Work: Salespeople’s Service Encounters in the Connected Store
Snippet: A plausible explanation for this statement is that a large proportion of the retail organisations in the research had developed from connected service encounters towards servitised service encounters (Fig. 4); the digitalisation of frontline service in these workplaces brought new tasks and job positions that required FSEs to engage in workplace learning. Whether service organisations target automated or servitised service encounters, the future for FSEs with low literacy, numeracy, computer, and digital skills is precarious. It is also important to point out that connected service encounters (based on interactive digital service networks) are not yet widespread. Ultimately, if they lack the resources to adapt to rapid changes in the service organisation and adopt new service roles, FSEs in entry-level positions (e.g., retail, hospitality, customer service) will be marginalised in the connected and servitised service encounter (cf. Barocas and Levy 2016;Ikeler 2016;Nickson et al. 2012). 

The postdigital seeks to understand how humans and technology relate to one another beyond binaries: 'we are increasingly no longer in a world where digital technology and Fig. 4 The evolution of FSEs' service encounters, from organic to postdigital dialogue media is separate, virtual other to a natural human and social life' (Jandrić et al. 2018). The findings in this study show that the practice traditions that reproduce salespeople's service encounters over time are resistant to change. Despite the retail chain organisations' efforts to implement in-situ technologies intended for use by customers and salespeople on the shopfloor, the salespeople reproduced service encounters defined as a game between people (Solomon et al. 1985), characterised by organic dialogue and emotional labour skills. At checkout, the service encounter transformed into what I define as a game between people and interactive technology, a connected service encounter characterised by 'postdigital dialogue' (Jandrić et al. 2019). The checkout process involved two parts, namely transactions and customer service. Three roles connected to transactions were identified: the enabler, translator, and coordinator (see Bowen 2016).

Title: Digitalization of relational space in the service triangle: The case study of retail banking
Snippet: Against the backdrop of these debates, our paper is focused on the progressive digitalization of the retail banking industry and its consequences on the relational space of work in the service triangle (Korczynski, 2009(Korczynski, , 2013;;Lopez, 2010;Gabriel et al., 2015). The retail banking sector is one of those in which the redesign of the relationship between supply and demand for services is more sensitive to the changes enabled by digitalization and learning algorithms, yet scholars have paid little attention to this subset of the financial sector. One consequence of digitization is the reduction of retail bank branches and a renewal of job profiles to support the digital transformation in central offices. Little attention has been given to the transformation of work and skills among the remaining retail bank employees. In this article, we aim to portray the workplace experience as it is understood by the retail workers themselves. Importantly, traditional skills not only need to be combined with digital ones, but they must also align with the new strategic objectives of the banking institutions. In fact, technological innovation is part of a path of great change that the banking sector has undergone in recent decades, as shown in the literature. Growing managerialization, globalization and increasing competition with actors other than banks have markedly changed employment practices and the way work is traditionally performed in the banking industry: studies from different countries have shown that a process of segmentation of work organization, accompanied by the narrowing of task variation, work intensification, and Taylorization, especially for customer-facing jobs, together with increased managerial control and the strengthening of sales culture, is proven to cause worrying levels of stress, a sense of alienation and hard work identity, hence characterizing an occupation that was traditionally associated with high prestige, meaningful work and advanced technical knowledge and skills (Regini et al., 1999;McCabe, 2007McCabe, , 2009;;Gond et al., 2014;Kipping and Westerhuis, 2014;du Plessis and Just, 2022).

snippet.text: Against the backdrop of these debates, our paper is focused on the progressive digitalization of the retail banking industry and its consequences on the relational space of work in the service triangle (Korczynski, 2009(Korczynski, , 2013;;Lopez, 2010;Gabriel et al., 2015). The retail banking sector is one of those in which the redesign of the relationship between supply and demand for services is more sensitive to the changes enabled by digitalization and learning algorithms, yet scholars have paid little attention to this subset of the financial sector. One consequence of digitization is the reduction of retail bank branches and a renewal of job profiles to support the digital transformation in central offices. Little attention has been given to the transformation of work and skills among the remaining retail bank employees. In this article, we aim to portray the workplace experience as it is understood by the retail workers themselves. Importantly, traditional skills not only need to be combined with digital ones, but they must also align with the new strategic objectives of the banking institutions. In fact, technological innovation is part of a path of great change that the banking sector has undergone in recent decades, as shown in the literature. Growing managerialization, globalization and increasing competition with actors other than banks have markedly changed employment practices and the way work is traditionally performed in the banking industry: studies from different countries have shown that a process of segmentation of work organization, accompanied by the narrowing of task variation, work intensification, and Taylorization, especially for customer-facing jobs, together with increased managerial control and the strengthening of sales culture, is proven to cause worrying levels of stress, a sense of alienation and hard work identity, hence characterizing an occupation that was traditionally associated with high prestige, meaningful work and advanced technical knowledge and skills (Regini et al., 1999;McCabe, 2007McCabe, , 2009;;Gond et al., 2014;Kipping and Westerhuis, 2014;du Plessis and Just, 2022).

documents.snippet:
As such, studies empirically exploring the impacts of digital innovations on skills requirements in the valuation profession are limited. Hence, this study explored literature in the services industry from healthcare to business administration (e.g. accounting, finance, auditing, management, and marketing) to understand the nature of general changes in the services industry to facilitate the primary research process. An overview of extant property literature on digitalisation and skills development is presented in Table 2. Overall, new technologies are changing job designs across the services industry, and these developments present challenges and potential for the workforce (see Figure 1). 

So, digitalisation will continue to challenge the mere acquisition of soft and technical skills as sustainable use of new technologies requires human interventions, and such circumstances require aligning machine learning with human reasoning. Therefore, the importance of soft skills lies in their irreplaceability, even in robotic environments. Consequently, a balance of proficiency in soft and technical skills is imperative in the era of technological transformation (Poláková et al., 2023). For now, there will continue to be an increasing demand for efficiency and effectiveness in extensive data and information processing capabilities, which means that the workforce needs to know why, when, and how to use digital tools and systems to perform jobs that involve complex cognitive and metacognitive skills instead of basic ICT skills (Chinien & Boutin, 2011).

documents.snippet: The study reveals that digital transformation has brought about significant changes in the hospitality industry, with digital skills becoming a key component of the sector's competencies. Job advertisements emphasize the importance of building good relationships with guests and meeting their needs through communication skills, which include direct interaction with customers via email, instant messaging applications, and customer management platforms. Operational skills, which involve using hotel management software and other digital systems, are the second most sought-after requirement, yet they significantly contribute to operational efficiency and customer satisfaction. On the other hand, employers view informational skills as supplementary rather than essential during the employee selection process. The most sought-after positions are receptionists, requiring strong communication skills and efficient operational abilities, while maintenance positions, with their more specific duties not directly related to the day-to-day guest experience, are in lower demand. Required technologies include hotel management systems and office equipment packages. The use of the internet and digital tools, such as email, online telephony, and social media, is more common than metasearch engines, with email and online telephony playing a significant role in internal and external communications and social media in promotions and customer interactions. The digital skills developed involve communication through various digital channels, with a focus on telephone, WhatsApp, and email, which are crucial for effective communication and responsiveness to guest needs. In conclusion, digital transformation highlights the importance of digital communication and operational skills in the hospitality sector, with hotel companies needing to adapt training programs and update job specifications to meet the evolving demands of the industry and reduce the skills gap.

harder.brainstorming: The seed question asks for a distinction between two types of digital skills. A straightforward survey would retrieve workforce-development and digital-literacy literature, then organize findings into two buckets. This is retrieval-heavy but reasoning-light. To make it harder, I could: (1) embed a false premise that these are fundamentally different skill sets (when they may overlap significantly), (2) require synthesis across disciplines that frame digital skills differently (education, labor economics, HCI), (3) require reasoning about edge cases where the boundary blurs (e.g., data analysts, digital marketers), (4) ask for causal reasoning about skill transfer or training effectiveness, or (5) make it require reconciling conflicting taxonomies or measurement frameworks. Option (3) is promising: forcing the system to handle boundary cases requires reasoning about which skills belong where and why—not just listing examples from each category. The system would need to evaluate whether specific roles (data analyst, UX researcher, digital marketer) require 'general' or 'tech' skills, which demands reasoning about skill depth, context, and role requirements rather than pure retrieval. However, this adds complexity via 'and.' A cleaner approach: embed a subtle misconception that treating them as discrete categories is straightforward, when in reality the boundary is contested and framework-dependent. But the strongest option exploits that different research communities (education policy, labor economics, industry training) use incompatible frameworks to define and measure digital skills, yet no meta-analysis reconciles them. The system can retrieve multiple taxonomies but is bad at the reasoning needed to explain WHY they conflict.

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of where major research frameworks disagree on the boundary between “general workforce digital skills” and “technical job skills.” The disagreements cluster around scope (what counts as “general”), granularity (how general-to-specific mapping is handled), and measurement (how indices aggregate across general and technical components). Convergences also exist, notably around cross-cutting competencies and the integration of occupational taxonomies.

Scope: Should general digital skills include cognitive/ethical competencies or focus on tool- and task-specific technicalities?
- UNESCO/ITU typology versus OECD/DESI-style technical indices: UNESCO and ITU explicitly distinguish a layered skill stack—basic functional skills (access and operate), generic skills (use technologies meaningfully to create and collaborate), and higher-level skills (software creation, empowering/transformational uses). <cite id="a42186fc-1">UNESCO and ITU define basic functional digital skills as the ability to access and carry out basic operations; generic digital skills as using digital technologies meaningfully (e.g., creating and collaborating online); and higher-level skills as employing digital technology for software creation or transformational purposes</cite>. This treats cross-cutting creation, collaboration, problem solving, and critical evaluation as part of “digital skills” at non-trivial levels, pushing the general/technical boundary outward. 
- OECD/DESI and G20 Skills Strategy critique: OECD/G20 policy work emphasizes aligning education with employer needs and measuring skills in ways that capture technical tool use while excluding cognitive/ethical layers when the scope is narrowed; critiques note that such narrow definitions miss the cognitive and ethical dimensions and over-rely on proxies like internet usage. <cite id="7b689099-3">OECD’s G20 Skills Strategy aligns education programs with employer needs, but measurement approaches that narrowly define digital literacy focus on technical use of tools and exclude cognitive and ethical awareness; critiques argue such measures are misleading and not standardized</cite>. <cite id="a42186fc-1">OECD and DESI are cited in tandem with UNESCO/ITU distinctions between basic functional, generic, and higher-level digital skills</cite>. 
- EU DigComp: The EU’s DigComp 2.x consolidates cross-cutting knowledge, skills, and attitudes across five domains, explicitly including problem solving, safety, information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, and content creation (with programming referenced), thereby embedding cognitive/ethical/problem-solving competencies into “general digital competence.” <cite id="00b16010-3">DigComp defines six areas—information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, problem solving, and technical operational skills—covering evaluation of information, programming, collaboration, safety, and problem solving</cite>. <cite id="00b16010-4">DigComp’s components group 21 competences across five areas with eight proficiency levels; cross-framework reviews conclude that “technical competence” in other models is a generic, hard-to-assess ability akin to “using digital technologies meaningfully” for work/study/life</cite>. 
- Implication of disagreement: Frameworks that treat problem solving, critical evaluation, and ethical/secure use as core digital competence (UNESCO/ITU, DigComp, EU policy) situate more of the skill set under “general workforce digital skills,” whereas OECD/DESI-oriented technical indices and some SME-focused studies demarcate these as separate “technical” skill domains, often focusing on device/software operations and domain-specific toolchains. <cite id="00b16010-3">Programming and critical evaluation are included within DigComp’s content creation and information domains</cite> <cite id="a42186fc-1">SME literature distinguishes basic functional skills, generic skills, and higher-level empowering skills, aligning with definitions that separate technical operations from transformational use</cite>.

Granularity and linkage to occupations: general-to-specific pathways and job-embedded competencies
- Job-agnostic frameworks vs. job-embedded taxonomies: EU frameworks like DigComp and UNESCO ICT-CFT are international, proficiency-graded competency models; however, they are often decoupled from detailed occupational taxonomies, whereas ESCO/ANZSCO-based approaches integrate job-embedded competencies. <cite id="00b16010-2">UNESCO ICT CFT and DigCompEdu share international applicability and matrix or detailed competency structures; eTQF/UNESCO ICT CFT emphasize ICT centrally in early versions, evolving toward “Application of Digital Skills” subordinate to pedagogical skills</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-0">ESCO implements DigComp’s essential knowledge and skills directly in occupation profiles, enabling alignment of general digital competences to specific occupations, though ESCO does not specify proficiency levels</cite>. 
- Industry demand measurement: Labor market tools (O*NET, Skills-OVATE) quantify skill importance and proficiency by occupation, creating pressure to separate general enablers from job-specific technical skills; EU policy explicitly couples ESCO with DigComp to set occupational digital competence baselines. <cite id="7b689099-0">ESCO provides a common vocabulary and directly implemented DigComp competences in occupation definitions; O*NET indicates skill importance and proficiency levels by occupation, complementing ESCO</cite>. <cite id="a42186fc-4">CEDEFOP’s Skills-OVATE uses ESCO to analyze real-time job-ad data and identify skills demand and vacancies, highlighting digital skills as high demand across industries</cite>. 
- Disagreement: Frameworks differ on how granular the boundary should be and whether general competences should be mandated per occupation. UNESCO/ITU and DigComp emphasize cross-domain competencies without occupation-specific prescriptiveness; OECD/DESI and O*NET-style indices focus on aggregating technical skill demands across jobs, risking overemphasis on IT specialist shortages versus general workforce digital literacy. <cite id="a42186fc-1">UNESCO/ITU distinguish basic/functional, generic, and higher-level skills, while OECD/DESI emphasize measurement aligned to labor market needs and technical competencies</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-3">OECD/PIAAC treats problem solving as part of broader skills assessment but does not isolate a standardized digital literacy component; critiques warn that technical-only measures exclude cognitive/ethical dimensions</cite>.

Status of “technical operational skills” and “technical job skills”: general competence vs. domain-specific specialization
- EU meta-analyses and DigComp structure: Within DigComp, “technical operational skills” are explicitly listed alongside cross-cutting areas; empirical work groups competences into “applied skills” (problem solving, communication, technical/operational) and “theoretical/knowledge” components, indicating persistent ambiguity about whether operational tool use is general capability or technical specialization. <cite id="00b16010-3">DigComp includes a distinct “Technical Operational Skills” area (e.g., operating devices/applications, identifying/solving technical problems)</cite>. <cite id="00b16010-3">Empirical grouping treats applied skills—problem solving, communication, and technological skills—as distinct from theoretical knowledge, underscoring the boundary tension between operational/tool skills and higher-order competencies</cite>. <cite id="00b16010-4">Reviews highlight that “technical competence” is hard to assess and overlaps with general “use digital technologies meaningfully” competences</cite>. 
- UNESCO/ITU levels: The UNESCO/ITU scheme explicitly reserves “higher-level” skills for software creation and transformational uses, which policy and industry typically map to “technical job skills,” while “generic” and “basic functional” sit in the general workforce bucket. <cite id="a42186fc-1">Generic digital skills are meaningful/helpful uses (creating, collaborating online), while higher-level skills involve software creation and transformational purposes</cite>. 
- Disagreement: Some frameworks (OECD/DESI, O*NET/ESCO-aligned) classify operational tool use and domain-specific software competencies as job skills to be measured and supplied per occupation, whereas others (EU/UNESCO) integrate these operational abilities within broader “digital competence” levels, blurring the boundary and leading to divergent measurement emphasis. <cite id="7b689099-1">Definitions vary widely; OECD/DESI emphasize technical skills alongside UNESCO/ITU’s basic/functional, generic, and higher-level distinctions</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-2">Different definitions emphasize different skill areas, with some labeling digital literacy and others digital competence; operational/tool skills often overlap with cross-domain abilities</cite>.

Measurement and aggregation: indices and surveys that tilt the boundary
- DESI/PIAAC vs. UNESCO/ITU/DigComp: DESI aggregates indicators that capture ICT specialist shortages and technical skill demand; OECD’s Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC component) assesses problem solving with a digital subtask but does not standardize a digital-only index. This leads to indices that emphasize technical job skills and underweight cross-cutting digital literacies. <cite id="7b689099-1">DESI is cited alongside OECD for tracking digital skills, with UNESCO/ITU definitions differentiating basic, generic, and higher-level skills</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-3">PIAAC’s problem-solving module includes digital information access/evaluation, yet critiques argue that measurement frameworks risk excluding cognitive/ethical dimensions and over-relying on proxies</cite>. 
- EU policy metrics: EU targets for basic digital skills for the general population and a parallel target for ICT specialists reveal a policy-driven boundary that separates general workforce competencies from technical job skills in planning and funding. <cite id="a42186fc-3">EU policy sets targets for 80% basic digital skills and for 20 million ICT specialists, underpinning a dual focus on general digital competences and specialized technical skills</cite>. <cite id="a42186fc-4">ESCO/CEDEFOP tools align general competences with occupational demand, reinforcing the general-to-technical mapping in policy execution</cite>. 
- Disagreement: Frameworks differ on whether digital skills indices should normalize out technical specialist components, how to weight cognitive/ethical/problem-solving subskills, and whether to report proficiency levels across occupations (DigComp/UNESCO) or aggregate only job-relevant technical competencies (DESI/O*NET). <cite id="7b689099-0">ESCO integrates DigComp competences into occupations without proficiency levels, creating a hybrid between general and job-specific reporting</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-3">OECD/G20 emphasize alignment with employer needs and warn that narrow technical measurement misses broader digital literacy components</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of where major research frameworks disagree on the boundary between “general workforce digital skills” and “technical job skills.” The disagreements cluster around scope (what counts as “general”), granularity (how general-to-specific mapping is handled), and measurement (how indices aggregate across general and technical components). Scope: Should general digital skills include cognitive/ethical competencies or focus on tool- and task-specific technicalities?
- UNESCO/ITU typology versus OECD/DESI-style technical indices: UNESCO and ITU explicitly distinguish a layered skill stack—basic functional skills (access and operate), generic skills (use technologies meaningfully to create and collaborate), and higher-level skills (software creation, empowering/transformational uses). <cite id="a42186fc-1">UNESCO and ITU define basic functional digital skills as the ability to access and carry out basic operations; generic digital skills as using digital technologies meaningfully (e.g., creating and collaborating online); and higher-level skills as employing digital technology for software creation or transformational purposes</cite>. This treats cross-cutting creation, collaboration, problem solving, and critical evaluation as part of “digital skills” at non-trivial levels, pushing the general/technical boundary outward. 
- OECD/DESI and G20 Skills Strategy critique: OECD/G20 policy work emphasizes aligning education with employer needs and measuring skills in ways that capture technical tool use while excluding cognitive/ethical layers when the scope is narrowed; critiques note that such narrow definitions miss the cognitive and ethical dimensions and over-rely on proxies like internet usage. <cite id="7b689099-3">OECD’s G20 Skills Strategy aligns education programs with employer needs, but measurement approaches that narrowly define digital literacy focus on technical use of tools and exclude cognitive and ethical awareness; critiques argue such measures are misleading and not standardized</cite>. <cite id="a42186fc-1">OECD and DESI are cited in tandem with UNESCO/ITU distinctions between basic functional, generic, and higher-level digital skills</cite>. 
- EU DigComp: The EU’s DigComp 2.x consolidates cross-cutting knowledge, skills, and attitudes across five domains, explicitly including problem solving, safety, information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, and content creation (with programming referenced), thereby embedding cognitive/ethical/problem-solving competencies into “general digital competence.” <cite id="00b16010-3">DigComp defines six areas—information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, problem solving, and technical operational skills—covering evaluation of information, programming, collaboration, safety, and problem solving</cite>. <cite id="00b16010-4">DigComp’s components group 21 competences across five areas with eight proficiency levels; cross-framework reviews conclude that “technical competence” in other models is a generic, hard-to-assess ability akin to “using digital technologies meaningfully” for work/study/life</cite>. 
- Implication of disagreement: Frameworks that treat problem solving, critical evaluation, and ethical/secure use as core digital competence (UNESCO/ITU, DigComp, EU policy) situate more of the skill set under “general workforce digital skills,” whereas OECD/DESI-oriented technical indices and some SME-focused studies demarcate these as separate “technical” skill domains, often focusing on device/software operations and domain-specific toolchains. <cite id="00b16010-3">Programming and critical evaluation are included within DigComp’s content creation and information domains</cite> <cite id="a42186fc-1">SME literature distinguishes basic functional skills, generic skills, and higher-level empowering skills, aligning with definitions that separate technical operations from transformational use</cite>.

Granularity and linkage to occupations: general-to-specific pathways and job-embedded competencies
- Job-agnostic frameworks vs. job-embedded taxonomies: EU frameworks like DigComp and UNESCO ICT-CFT are international, proficiency-graded competency models; however, they are often decoupled from detailed occupational taxonomies, whereas ESCO/ANZSCO-based approaches integrate job-embedded competencies. <cite id="00b16010-2">UNESCO ICT CFT and DigCompEdu share international applicability and matrix or detailed competency structures; eTQF/UNESCO ICT CFT emphasize ICT centrally in early versions, evolving toward “Application of Digital Skills” subordinate to pedagogical skills</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-0">ESCO implements DigComp’s essential knowledge and skills directly in occupation profiles, enabling alignment of general digital competences to specific occupations, though ESCO does not specify proficiency levels</cite>. 
- Industry demand measurement: Labor market tools (O*NET, Skills-OVATE) quantify skill importance and proficiency by occupation, creating pressure to separate general enablers from job-specific technical skills; EU policy explicitly couples ESCO with DigComp to set occupational digital competence baselines. <cite id="7b689099-0">ESCO provides a common vocabulary and directly implemented DigComp competences in occupation definitions; O*NET indicates skill importance and proficiency levels by occupation, complementing ESCO</cite>. <cite id="a42186fc-4">CEDEFOP’s Skills-OVATE uses ESCO to analyze real-time job-ad data and identify skills demand and vacancies, highlighting digital skills as high demand across industries</cite>. 
- Disagreement: Frameworks differ on how granular the boundary should be and whether general competences should be mandated per occupation. UNESCO/ITU and DigComp emphasize cross-domain competencies without occupation-specific prescriptiveness; OECD/DESI and O*NET-style indices focus on aggregating technical skill demands across jobs, risking overemphasis on IT specialist shortages versus general workforce digital literacy. <cite id="a42186fc-1">UNESCO/ITU distinguish basic/functional, generic, and higher-level skills, while OECD/DESI emphasize measurement aligned to labor market needs and technical competencies</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-3">OECD/PIAAC treats problem solving as part of broader skills assessment but does not isolate a standardized digital literacy component; critiques warn that technical-only measures exclude cognitive/ethical dimensions</cite>.

Status of “technical operational skills” and “technical job skills”: general competence vs. domain-specific specialization
- EU meta-analyses and DigComp structure: Within DigComp, “technical operational skills” are explicitly listed alongside cross-cutting areas; empirical work groups competences into “applied skills” (problem solving, communication, technical/operational) and “theoretical/knowledge” components, indicating persistent ambiguity about whether operational tool use is general capability or technical specialization. <cite id="00b16010-3">DigComp includes a distinct “Technical Operational Skills” area (e.g., operating devices/applications, identifying/solving technical problems)</cite>. <cite id="00b16010-3">Empirical grouping treats applied skills—problem solving, communication, and technological skills—as distinct from theoretical knowledge, underscoring the boundary tension between operational/tool skills and higher-order competencies</cite>. <cite id="00b16010-4">Reviews highlight that “technical competence” is hard to assess and overlaps with general “use digital technologies meaningfully” competences</cite>. 
- UNESCO/ITU levels: The UNESCO/ITU scheme explicitly reserves “higher-level” skills for software creation and transformational uses, which policy and industry typically map to “technical job skills,” while “generic” and “basic functional” sit in the general workforce bucket. <cite id="a42186fc-1">Generic digital skills are meaningful/helpful uses (creating, collaborating online), while higher-level skills involve software creation and transformational purposes</cite>. 
- Disagreement: Some frameworks (OECD/DESI, O*NET/ESCO-aligned) classify operational tool use and domain-specific software competencies as job skills to be measured and supplied per occupation, whereas others (EU/UNESCO) integrate these operational abilities within broader “digital competence” levels, blurring the boundary and leading to divergent measurement emphasis. <cite id="7b689099-1">Definitions vary widely; OECD/DESI emphasize technical skills alongside UNESCO/ITU’s basic/functional, generic, and higher-level distinctions</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-2">Different definitions emphasize different skill areas, with some labeling digital literacy and others digital competence; operational/tool skills often overlap with cross-domain abilities</cite>.

- DESI/PIAAC vs. UNESCO/ITU/DigComp: DESI aggregates indicators that capture ICT specialist shortages and technical skill demand; OECD’s Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC component) assesses problem solving with a digital subtask but does not standardize a digital-only index. - EU policy metrics: EU targets for basic digital skills for the general population and a parallel target for ICT specialists reveal a policy-driven boundary that separates general workforce competencies from technical job skills in planning and funding. <cite id="a42186fc-3">EU policy sets targets for 80% basic digital skills and for 20 million ICT specialists, underpinning a dual focus on general digital competences and specialized technical skills</cite>. <cite id="a42186fc-4">ESCO/CEDEFOP tools align general competences with occupational demand, reinforcing the general-to-technical mapping in policy execution</cite>. 
- Disagreement: Frameworks differ on whether digital skills indices should normalize out technical specialist components, how to weight cognitive/ethical/problem-solving subskills, and whether to report proficiency levels across occupations (DigComp/UNESCO) or aggregate only job-relevant technical competencies (DESI/O*NET). <cite id="7b689099-0">ESCO integrates DigComp competences into occupations without proficiency levels, creating a hybrid between general and job-specific reporting</cite>. <cite id="7b689099-3">OECD/G20 emphasize alignment with employer needs and warn that narrow technical measurement misses broader digital literacy components</cite>.

Convergences and practical implications
- Cross-cutting competencies: Despite disagreements, most frameworks converge on core cross-cutting abilities—information evaluation, communication/collaboration, content creation/problem solving, safety/ethics—as digital competence foundations that cut across jobs. <cite id="00b16010-3">DigComp’s five areas explicitly include information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving, with technical operational skills as a separate, but related, component</cite>. <cite id="00b16010-1">Regional frameworks emphasize 21st-century digital skills (critical thinking, problem solving, communication, collaboration, safety) as foundational</cite>. <cite id="00b16010-2">UNESCO ICT CFT evolved from ICT-centric models to “Application of Digital Skills” subordinate to pedagogical competencies, reinforcing cross-domain integration</cite>. 
- Occupational alignment: EU policy and CEDEFOP practice demonstrate a practical synthesis—using general frameworks (DigComp) to populate occupation profiles (ESCO) and then measuring demand via labor market data, which narrows the general–technical gap in policy operations even when conceptual boundaries remain contested. <cite id="7b689099-0">ESCO directly implements DigComp in occupation definitions, enabling job-embedded digital competence baselines</cite>. <cite id="a42186fc-4">Skills-OVATE operationalizes demand-driven digital skill development across industries</cite>. 
- Policy design guidance: Where frameworks disagree, program designers face choices—whether to prioritize broad digital literacy indices that include cognitive/ethical/problem-solving competencies or to emphasize technical indices like DESI that capture specialist shortages; the evidence suggests both are needed, with careful calibration to avoid misclassification and measurement bias. <cite id="7b689099-3">Narrow technical-only measures miss cognitive/ethical aspects and proxy pitfalls, suggesting indices should broaden beyond tool-use metrics</cite>. <cite id="a42186fc-1">UNESCO/ITU’s layered model provides conceptual boundaries to separate basic/functional, generic, and higher-level skills, aiding targeted policy</cite>.

Title: A digital competence framework for learners (DCFL): A conceptual framework for digital literacy
Snippet: Digital technologies are the main driver of the future economy, with technology jobs and those requiring digital skills on the rise. In educational settings, there is an accelerated propagation of digital learning environments, which was amplified by the online shift following COVID-19. To equip learners with the necessary digital skills, there ought to be a purpose-built framework that can be used as a reference point. Although in recent years there were multiple attempts to develop digital literacy frameworks such as DigComp by the European Commission and the Digital Literacy Global Framework (DLGF) by UNESCO, with several other frameworks built on top of them, there is a lack of frameworks devised specifically for learners and students. This paper proposes a conceptual digital literacy framework for learners, building mainly on DigComp 2.0 and the DLGF. We use an integrative review methodology of six main empirical frameworks, developed in recent years with educational applications, to achieve our aim. We added new competencies specific to mobile learning environments and career-related digital endeavors by learners. In addition, we further tailored the competences related to device and software operations to both personal computers and mobile devices. The proposed framework in this paper expounds on DigComp and DLGF by adding several competences which are deemed essential for learners in today’s digital world. The framework can be used by educational institutes, policymakers, as well as learners to assess their digital skills and devise strategies for capacity building.

Title: Digital Competences of Digital Natives: Measuring Skills in the Modern Technology Environment
Snippet: The EU has set ambitious targets for 2030, aiming to ensure at least 80% of the population possesses basic digital skills and to have 20 million ICT specialists. These targets align with the Digital Compass for Europe's digital decade and the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan. Also, digital skills for work and for life are at the top of the European Policy Agenda. The European Skills Agenda, of 1 July 2020, supports digital skills for all, supporting the objectives of the Digital Education Action Plan, which has the objectives of (i) enhancing digital skills and competences for the digital transformation while (ii) fostering the development of a high-performing digital education system [38]. 

To meet the set goals the European Commission defined a common set of digital competences that individuals need to possess, regardless of their level of digital expertise and it systemized them as a reference for policymakers, educators and individuals to understand and develop digital skills. The "Digital Competence Framework for Citizens", or DigComp, is a reference framework introduced in 2013 based on a survey of experts' views on digital competences [39]. Since then, there have been further updates and revisions of the framework to adapt to the changing digital landscape and technological advances. The DigComp 2.2 update in 2022 involved extensive consultation with various stakeholders through a dedicated community of practitioners. Open validation processes included input from key international organisations (such as International Labour Organization, UNESCO, United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund and the World Bank) aimed at addressing citizens' knowledge, skills and attitudes in response to evolving technological landscapes and incorporating considerations for green and sustainable interaction with digital technologies. 

The framework has been put into practise at the EU level to produce the Digital Skills Indicator (DSI), which is used to set policy targets and monitor the Digital Economy and Society Indicator (DESI). It is also integrated into the Europass curriculum vitae (CV) template, which allows job seekers to assess their own digital skills and include the assessment in their respective CV. 

DigComp includes five key dimensions with detailed descriptors for the competence levels (basic, intermediate, advanced and highly specialised) and examples of knowledge, skills and attitudes for each competence.

Title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF ECONOMIES THROUGH TECHNOLOGY, EDUCATION AND COMPETENCES
Snippet: Forty-two percent of Europeans, representing 37% of the total workforce, lack this skill, indicating a significant lack of digital skills in Europe (European Commission, 2023). Only 54% of Europeans aged 16-74 have basic digital skills, in 2021, 1 in 6 Europeans had no digital skills (European Commission, 2022a). In order for Europe to achieve the European Digital Decade goal of 80% of the European population having at least basic digital skills by 2030, additional efforts and investments in digital education are urgently needed to improve the digital skills of Europeans (European Commission, 2022a). To be able to follow the market demands, the European Center for the Development of Vocational Education and Training (CEDEFOP, 2024) created an online vacancy analysis tool called Skills-OVATE, which uses the ESCO classification of skills, competences and occupations (European Commission, 2024), to improve labor market transparency and facilitate policy making. This tool uses big data and provides detailed information on skills demand and vacancies (OJAs) based on real-time data from millions of job advertisements on thousands of private job portals, public employment job portals and recruitment agency portals (CEDEFOP, 2024). OJA's latest data indicates that digital skills are among those in the highest demand across all industries. 

Consequently, digital competences of the workforce should be developed not only at educational institutions but also at the workplaces (Uzule & Kuzmina-Merlino, 2022). To synchronize training standards, various digital competence frameworks have been designed, including the DigComp framework of the Department of Education and the European Commission (Audrin et al., 2024;Vuorikari et al., 2022) due to the necessity to improve digital skills of all citizens by 2030 (European Commission, 2022b). 

At the organizational level, successful digital transformations depend on the digital competencies of both the workforce and managers. Specifically, digital transformations require significant financial resources and organizational change (Geada et al., 2023), and it is up to managers to understand how to organize these processes.

documents.title: A digital competence framework for learners (DCFL): A conceptual framework for digital literacy
documents.snippet: Digital technologies are the main driver of the future economy, with technology jobs and those requiring digital skills on the rise. In educational settings, there is an accelerated propagation of digital learning environments, which was amplified by the online shift following COVID-19. To equip learners with the necessary digital skills, there ought to be a purpose-built framework that can be used as a reference point. Although in recent years there were multiple attempts to develop digital literacy frameworks such as DigComp by the European Commission and the Digital Literacy Global Framework (DLGF) by UNESCO, with several other frameworks built on top of them, there is a lack of frameworks devised specifically for learners and students. This paper proposes a conceptual digital literacy framework for learners, building mainly on DigComp 2.0 and the DLGF. We use an integrative review methodology of six main empirical frameworks, developed in recent years with educational applications, to achieve our aim. We added new competencies specific to mobile learning environments and career-related digital endeavors by learners. In addition, we further tailored the competences related to device and software operations to both personal computers and mobile devices. The proposed framework in this paper expounds on DigComp and DLGF by adding several competences which are deemed essential for learners in today’s digital world. The framework can be used by educational institutes, policymakers, as well as learners to assess their digital skills and devise strategies for capacity building.

Title: Is there a gender gap? A meta-analysis of the gender differences in students' ICT literacy
Snippet: The existing frameworks of ICT literacy outline the knowledge and skills students need in order to become digitally literate. Although these frameworks are diverse and structured differently, they converge to a great extent to a set of core knowledge domains and skills of ICT literacy (Voogt & Roblin, 2012). The so-called DIGCOMP (Developing and Understanding Digital Competence in Europe) framework, which was initially developed by the European Commission (Ferrari, 2013) and revised in a recently published systematic review (Siddiq et al., 2016), describes these domains and skills: The revised DIGCOMP framework postulates six areas: Information, Communication, Content Creation, Safety, Problem Solving, and Technical Operational Skills, and each area further consists of several competences. For instance, Information includes competences such as search for-and use of information, storing and retrieving information, including evaluation of information. Content Creation includes the knowledge and skills to develop new ideas or content and redefine existing ones. Moreover, programming and acknowledging copyright and licenses are also included in this competence areas. Communication is related to interaction with others, both synchronously and asynchronously, and includes collaboration, a competence needed to participate and contribute to teams using ICT, and to participate in and create social networks. Safety includes competences related to protecting personal data, health, devices and the environment. Moreover, netiquette is an important aspect of this area. Problem solving includes innovating and creatively using technology and solving problems individually or collaboratively. At last, Technical Operational Skills include generic ICT skills, such as operating devices and applications and identifying and solving technical problems. 

Furthermore, to facilitate the present meta-analysis, the test content was recorded by further dividing these competence areas along with the task descriptions into two main groups: (1) applied skills, which consist of the skills that require the test-taker to apply knowledge to solve a problem or come to a solution by taking several actions (i.e., problem solving, communication and technological skills), and (2) other skills, which consist of competence or knowledge the students have and was shown by providing answers to tasks without taking further actions (i.e., knowledge-lean and theoretical skills).

The existing frameworks of ICT literacy outline the knowledge and skills students need in order to become digitally literate. Although these frameworks are diverse and structured differently, they converge to a great extent to a set of core knowledge domains and skills of ICT literacy (Voogt & Roblin, 2012). The so-called DIGCOMP (Developing and Understanding Digital Competence in Europe) framework, which was initially developed by the European Commission (Ferrari, 2013) and revised in a recently published systematic review (Siddiq et al., 2016), describes these domains and skills: The revised DIGCOMP framework postulates six areas: Information, Communication, Content Creation, Safety, Problem Solving, and Technical Operational Skills, and each area further consists of several competences. For instance, Information includes competences such as search for-and use of information, storing and retrieving information, including evaluation of information. Content Creation includes the knowledge and skills to develop new ideas or content and redefine existing ones. Moreover, programming and acknowledging copyright and licenses are also included in this competence areas. Communication is related to interaction with others, both synchronously and asynchronously, and includes collaboration, a competence needed to participate and contribute to teams using ICT, and to participate in and create social networks. Safety includes competences related to protecting personal data, health, devices and the environment. Moreover, netiquette is an important aspect of this area. Problem solving includes innovating and creatively using technology and solving problems individually or collaboratively. At last, Technical Operational Skills include generic ICT skills, such as operating devices and applications and identifying and solving technical problems. 

Furthermore, to facilitate the present meta-analysis, the test content was recorded by further dividing these competence areas along with the task descriptions into two main groups: (1) applied skills, which consist of the skills that require the test-taker to apply knowledge to solve a problem or come to a solution by taking several actions (i.e., problem solving, communication and technological skills), and (2) other skills, which consist of competence or knowledge the students have and was shown by providing answers to tasks without taking further actions (i.e., knowledge-lean and theoretical skills).
